notes.title: Propositions and truth values
Truth tables, computed by enumeration
De Morgan's laws, verified by brute force
Implication and the contrapositive
notes.body: `p -> q` (if p then q) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive `(NOT q) -> (NOT p)`. Worked verification: all 4 assignments agree — **True**. The converse `q -> p` is NOT equivalent (check p=T,q=F: implication false, converse true). Practical use: to prove 'if the build passes then tests ran', prove the contrapositive 'if tests did not run then the build fails' — often the easier direction. Confusing implication with converse is one of the most common logic errors in specifications.

notes.title: Predicate logic over finite domains
notes.body: Predicates add quantifiers: `FORALL x, P(x)` and `EXISTS x, P(x)`. Over a finite domain you can evaluate them by enumeration. Worked example: domain = {2, 3, 4}, statement `EXISTS x, x is prime AND x > 3`. Check: x=2 (prime, not >3, fails), x=3 (prime, not >3, fails), x=4 (not prime, fails). No witness exists, so the statement is **false**. Change `>3` to `>=3`: x=3 is prime and >= 3, so the statement becomes **true**. Existence claims need exactly one witness; universal claims need every case. This discipline maps directly onto testing: 'there exists an input that crashes' vs 'for all inputs it terminates'.

notes.body: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average. Worked example: a retry policy succeeds on attempt 1 with p=0.7, attempt 2 with p=0.2, attempt 3 with p=0.1 (then gives up). Expected attempts = 1×0.7 + 2×0.2 + 3×0.1 = **1.4000000000000001**. Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when X,Y are dependent — the workhorse for analyzing total cost, total latency, total errors across components without modeling their joint distribution.

notes.title: The binomial distribution, computed
notes.body: P(X=k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k). Worked example: 10 requests, each fails independently with p=0.5 (a coin). P(exactly 3 fail) = C(10,3)×0.5^3×0.5^7 = 120×0.5^10 = **0.1172**. Sanity: probabilities over k=0..10 sum to 1.000000 = 1 ✓. Use the binomial for 'k of n independent trials' questions — canary failures, bit errors, A/B conversions.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: - **Function** — a rule assigning each input exactly one output; the core object of algebra — domain, range, composition, inverses. - **Exponential and logarithm** — an inverse pair, the growth/decay language; change of base: log_a(b) = ln b / ln a. - **Unit circle** — x²+y²=1; every trigonometric identity lives here. - **Complex number** — a+bi, the algebraic closure: every polynomial equation has its solutions here. - **Limit** — the value a function approaches; continuity and the derivative both rest on the epsilon-delta idea. - **Derivative** — the instantaneous rate of change; definition → rules → the chain rule. - **Chain rule** — (f∘g)′ = f′(g(x))·g′(x); the whole game in disguise — backprop is the chain rule at scale. - **Integral** — accumulated area; the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums. - **Fundamental Theorem** — differentiation and integration are inverses: ∫ₐᵇ f′ = f(b)−f(a). - **Series** — an infinite sum; convergence decided by tests — p-series (converges iff p>1), ratio, comparison. - **Taylor series** — the local polynomial approximation f(x) ≈ Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!; bound the error with the Lagrange remainder. - **Induction** — proof by domino: base case → hypothesis → step. - **Proof by contradiction** — assume the negation, derive the absurd; the contrapositive rides alongside. - **Pigeonhole principle** — n+1 items in n boxes forces a box with two or more; deceptively powerful. - **Combinatorics** — organized counting: every 'how many' reduces to product rule, sum rule, and choose. - **Graph** — vertices and edges; the universal model — paths, cycles, trees, coloring, Euler/Hamilton. When stuck, draw the graph. - **Modular arithmetic** — arithmetic on remainders; the road to RSA. - **Finite automaton** — the simplest computation model; the preview of theory. - **Eigenvalue/eigenvector** — the scalar λ and direction v with Av = λv: where the matrix acts by pure scaling — PCA, PageRank, quantum states. - **Least squares** — the projection of the data onto the model space; the geometry of regression. - **SVD** — A = UΣVᵀ, the everything-decomposition: rank, compression, latent factors. - **Matrix calculus** — gradients of vector-valued functions; the language ML optimizers speak. - **Distribution** — the zoo: normal, binomial, Poisson, exponential; know each one's story. - **Bayes' theorem** — P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E); the update rule for all reasoning under uncertainty. - **MLE/MAP** — fit by maximizing likelihood (MLE), or likelihood × prior (MAP). - **Law of large numbers** — sample averages converge to the expectation; frequencies become probabilities. - **Central limit theorem** — sums of many small independent effects go normal; the reason normal distributions are everywhere. - **Regression and hypothesis testing** — fit the model, then ask whether the fit means anything; p-values and confidence intervals — and their misuses.

notes.body:
**Problem.** d/dx [x³·sin x]?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** 3x² sin x + x³ cos x
- **Why:** The product rule — see 'Concepts': (uv)' = u'v + uv'.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *The product rule — see 'Concepts': (uv)' = u'v + uv'.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

I'm your instructor, and this first module is the whole reason this course exists: the unified mathematical spine — college algebra through probability and statistics, in the verified course order. We climb it together: equations and functions, trigonometry and the unit circle, precalculus (complex numbers, vectors, the limits preview), calculus I (limits, derivatives, integrals, the Fundamental Theorem), calculus II (integration techniques, series, Taylor), discrete mathematics (logic, proofs, combinatorics, graphs), linear algebra (eigenvalues, least squares, SVD, matrix calculus for ML), and probability and statistics (distributions, Bayes and MLE/MAP, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, regression, hypothesis testing). I gate every node at mastery: no calculus without functions, no machine learning without linear algebra.

Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Mathematics is unforgiving of process errors. In Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance, these habits cost more points than lack of talent:
- **Writing equations before defining variables.** Name every symbol before you use it. Half of all 'I got stuck' moments in Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance are really 'I never said what x was.'
- **Unit blindness.** Numbers without units are ornaments. Carry units through every step and check that the final unit matches what the question asked for — especially in trade and finance contexts.
- **Never checking.** Plug the answer back in. Estimate first, compute second, verify third. An unchecked answer in Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance is a guess with extra steps.
- **Formula hunting instead of deriving.** Memorizing ten special cases instead of one general principle. When memory fails under pressure, derivation still works.
- **Precision theater.** More decimal places do not mean more accuracy. Report precision honestly — it cannot exceed the precision of your inputs.
- **Skipping the easy problems.** Fluency comes from volume at the edge of comfort, not from staring at one hard problem. Do the reps.

scriptLabs.title: Taylor Approximation Laboratory
scriptLabs.brief: Approximate sin(x) with Taylor polynomials of degree 1, 3, 5, 7 at x=0.5; compute actual errors and the Lagrange bound. See convergence happen.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math

def taylor_sin(x, n):
    # YOUR TASK: sum_{k=0..n} (-1)^k x^(2k+1) / (2k+1)!
    pass

x = 0.5
for n in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    approx = taylor_sin(x, n)
    print(f'degree {2*n+1}: approx={approx:.10f} error={abs(approx-math.sin(x)):.2e}')
scriptLabs.hint: term k: (-1)**k * x**(2*k+1) / math.factorial(2*k+1). n=0 → degree 1, n=3 → degree 7.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math

def taylor_sin(x, n):
    return sum((-1)**k * x**(2*k+1) / math.factorial(2*k+1) for k in range(n+1))

x = 0.5
for n in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    approx = taylor_sin(x, n)
    err = abs(approx - math.sin(x))
    # Lagrange bound: |R| <= |x|^(2n+3)/(2n+3)!
    bound = abs(x)**(2*n+3) / math.factorial(2*n+3)
    print(f'degree {2*n+1}: approx={approx:.10f} error={err:.2e} bound={bound:.2e}')
# Lesson: error collapses as degree grows — approximation with guarantees.

scriptLabs.title: Monte Carlo: π and Confidence
scriptLabs.brief: Estimate π by dart-throwing; show the estimate converging as N grows; compute a 95% confidence interval. Simulation as a numerical method.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math, random

def estimate_pi(n):
    # YOUR TASK: n darts in [0,1]^2, count inside quarter circle
    pass

for n in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    est = estimate_pi(n)
    print(f'N={n}: pi~{est:.5f} error={abs(est-math.pi):.2e}')
scriptLabs.hint: inside if x*x+y*y<=1. pi ≈ 4*inside/n. SE ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)*4; 95% CI ≈ est ± 1.96*SE.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math, random

def estimate_pi(n):
    inside = sum(1 for _ in range(n)
                 if (lambda x, y: x*x + y*y <= 1)(random.random(), random.random()))
    return 4*inside/n

for n in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    est = estimate_pi(n)
    p = est/4
    se = 4*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
    print(f'N={n}: pi~{est:.5f} err={abs(est-math.pi):.2e} 95%CI=({est-1.96*se:.4f},{est+1.96*se:.4f})')
# Lesson: error shrinks as 1/sqrt(N) — the Monte Carlo rate; CIs quantify it.

scriptLabs.title: Least Squares from Scratch
scriptLabs.brief: Fit y = ax + b to noisy data via the normal equations — no libraries. Then verify against the closed form. The geometry of regression, by hand.
scriptLabs.starter:
# data: noisy line
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
ys = [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1]
# YOUR TASK: solve [sum x^2, sum x; sum x, n] [a; b] = [sum x*y; sum y]  (normal equations)
# print a, b
scriptLabs.solution:
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
ys = [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1]
n = len(xs)
sx, sy = sum(xs), sum(ys)
sxx, sxy = sum(x*x for x in xs), sum(x*y for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
# normal equations: a = (n*Sxy - Sx*Sy)/(n*Sxx - Sx^2)
den = n*sxx - sx*sx
a = (n*sxy - sx*sy)/den
b = (sy - a*sx)/n
print(f'y = {a:.4f}x + {b:.4f}')  # ~ y = 2x + 0.1
# Lesson: least squares is projection — the normal equations are geometry, not magic.

cheatSheets.title: The spine — algebra through probability in one page

blocks.body: Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a. Completing the square reveals vertex form. Exponent rules: xᵃ·xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ, (xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ, x⁻ᵃ = 1/xᵃ.
log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y; log_b(xᵏ) = k·log_b x; change of base: log_b x = ln x / ln b. Logs turn multiplication into addition.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Unit circle: angle → (cos, sin). Radians = arc length; π rad = 180°.
Derivative = instantaneous rate of change; d/dx[xⁿ] = nxⁿ⁻¹. Integral = accumulated area; ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). Fundamental theorem: they undo each other.
Induction: base case + step. Combinations C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!). Pigeonhole: n+1 items in n boxes → a shared box.
Matrix = linear map. Ax = b solvable ⟺ b in column space. Determinant = volume scaling factor; zero ⟺ singular.
P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B) (Bayes). E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] always. Variance adds only for independent variables.

cheatSheets.title: SQ3R — reading technical material that fights back

blocks.body: Skim headings, figures, and summaries first. Build the skeleton before the flesh: what is this chapter *for*?
Turn each heading into a question. 'The chain rule' → 'How do I differentiate a composition, and why does multiplying derivatives work?'
Read to answer your questions. Mark — don't highlight everything. One margin note per page maximum.
Close the book. State the answer aloud or on blank paper. If you can't reproduce it, you haven't read it.
Within 24 hours, re-derive the key results from memory. Spaced re-derivation beats re-reading 10-to-1.

cheatSheets.title: Time and risk — the quant prerequisites

blocks.body: PV = FV / (1+r)ᵗ. Money later is worth less; the discount rate r is the price of waiting.
E[X] = Σ x·P(x). Price of a gamble = its expectation under the risk-neutral measure; your edge is expectation minus price.
Var(X) = E[X²] − E[X]². Standard deviation σ is the native unit of risk; returns scale with √t over time.
68–95–99.7 rule: ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ. Z-score = (x − μ)/σ converts any normal to standard.
A random walk's distance grows like √t, not t. That square-root is why option value and risk both scale sublinearly with time.

answerBank.q: Where do I start if math is rusty?
answerBank.a: The placement diagnostic — usually Module 2 (tech math) for fluency, then the spine from college algebra. Don't start calculus with shaky algebra; the gate exists to save you months.

answerBank.q: How much math for machine learning?
answerBank.a: Linear algebra (vectors, eigenvalues, SVD), probability (Bayes, distributions, MLE), calculus (gradients, chain rule). That's Module 1's back half — the platform gates IL-07/IL-16 on these nodes.
They're a writing skill: do every exercise, read proofs actively (cover the next line, predict it), and keep a proof journal. Induction first — it's the most mechanical, and it builds the muscle.

answerBank.q: Is the electrician track only for electricians?
answerBank.a: The math (DC theory, shop math) and reading (SQ3R, code literacy) transfer to any trade. The etA credential sequence is electrician-specific; the study skills are universal.

answerBank.q: Quant math without a finance background?
answerBank.a: Yes — the module is prerequisites, not trading. Measure theory, stochastic processes, and time value of money are the language; the ladder (in IL-10's quant track) comes after.
By hand until fluent, then calculator for speed. Exams and job sites test the fluency; the tool is for after you understand.

faq.q: I'm bad at math. Can this course actually fix that?
faq.a: It targets exactly that: arithmetic fluency under time first, then the spine topic by topic. 'Bad at math' is usually 'rusty at arithmetic and never taught to read proofs' — both are trainable, and the course is sequenced for it.

faq.q: Why is there an electrician-apprenticeship module in a math course?
faq.a: The etA entrance exam is a concrete, high-stakes applied-math target (trade math: fractions, conduit bends, Ohm's law). It gives the abstract spine a real exam to aim at.

faq.q: Do I need calculus before probability?
faq.a: For this course's probability: no. Discrete probability (counting, Bayes, expectation) needs only algebra. Continuous distributions use integrals later, and the course sequences it that way.
The study guide paces it, but the rule is: 25-minute fluency drills daily (non-negotiable) plus one spine topic block. Fluency is a daily practice, not a weekly event.

faq.q: What's the difference between this and IL-20 (Mathematics)?
faq.a: IL-02 is the *engine*: fluency, study method, and the spine at working depth, aimed at trades/quant readiness. IL-20 is the fuller formal treatment (proofs, linear algebra III, multivariable calculus, numerical methods). Take IL-02 first if you're rusty.

faq.q: Why SQ3R instead of just reading?
faq.a: Technical text is not narrative — passive reading produces the illusion of understanding. Recite-from-blank-paper is the only honest check, and it's built into the method.

faq.q: Is the quant-finance module enough to get a quant job?
faq.a: No — it's explicitly *prerequisites*: stochastic processes and financial math as the on-ramp to the quant ladder (MicroMasters → interviews), not the ladder itself. IL-10's career track continues it.
Fluency drills: no calculator, that's the point. Spine topics: calculator allowed once the concept is hand-verified. Exams decide the rest — practice both ways.

freshSignals.headline: MIT 18.01SC Single Variable Calculus folded into the math spine
freshSignals.brief: MIT's OCW Scholar edition of Single Variable Calculus (Prof. David Jerison, Fall 2010) is now linked as a foundational spine resource. Five units take you from differentiation rules through optimization and related rates, into definite integrals and their applications (areas, volumes, work), then integration techniques (trig substitution, partial fractions, parts), closing with infinite series and Taylor expansions. About 150 hours of sessions, problem sets, and exams with solutions, built for independent study.

sources.label: MIT OCW Introductory Science & Math collection

freshSignals.noahPrompt: Ask Noah to build you a study plan through 18.01SC's five units, or to drill you on any one: chain rule, optimization, u-substitution, or Taylor series approximations.

freshSignals.headline: MIT 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus added to the math spine
freshSignals.brief: MIT's OCW Scholar Multivariable Calculus extends the 18.01 foundation to functions of several variables: partial derivatives, multiple integrals, and vector calculus (line/surface integrals, gradient, divergence, curl, Stokes' and divergence theorems). These are the tools behind physics simulations, engineering analysis, economics models, and computer graphics. Includes lecture and recitation videos, interactive Mathlets applets, worked examples, problem sets, and exams with solutions.
